questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical multitenant QoS design under bursty traffic and storms.

## Key Concepts
- Per-tenant rate limiting with token buckets
- Deficit Round Robin (DRR) scheduling
- Backpressure signaling and per-tenant buffers
- Observability: tail latency, SLA guards, isolation proofs

## Code Example
```javascript
// Pseudo token bucket limiter
class TokenBucket { constructor(rate, burst) { this.rate = rate; this.burst = burst; this.tokens = burst; this.last = Date.now(); }
  consume(n) { this.refill(); if (this.tokens >= n) { this.tokens -= n; return true; } return false; }
  refill() { const now = Date.now(); const add = ((now - this.last) / 1000) * this.rate; this.tokens = Math.min(this.burst, this.tokens + add); this.last = now; }
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle tenants joining/leaving and dynamic SLA changes?
- How do you detect and mitigate misbehaving tenants without impacting others?

questions.explanation: This design leverages Kafka's built-in quota system rather than custom credits. Key Kafka-native mechanisms: quotas enforced at brokers viaQuotaManager handle per-client throttling without application-level credits. Latency tracking uses record header timestamps enabling end-to-end measurement. Backpressure signals use FetchResponse throttle-time and TooManyRequestsException to push back. Fairness uses Kafka's bandwidth allocation algorithms, not basic credit-bucket. Test plan includes chaos (node failures) testing fault tolerance under the KCNA emphasis on operational robustness. Kafka broker quotas are the correct data-plane mechanism, not middleware credit systems.
